claim: Competition geometry problems can be automatically translated into Lean 4 statements that use only standard mathlib (the plane as two-dimensional Euclidean space, no custom axioms or external solvers), at the scale of hundreds of thousands of problems, if a language model is made to state explicitly the non-degeneracy and configuration assumptions that informal geometry leaves implicit: retrieving mathlib definitions together with the side conditions each needs, sketching an informal proof first to commit to a configuration, and repairing statements from compiler errors. Supported only if at least 95% of problems in both a 780-problem olympiad set and a 184K-problem web-scale set get at least one compiling statement; if expert annotators judge the first of five compiling candidates faithful for at least 45% of 180 competition problems of difficulty 4 or above and at least one of the five faithful for at least 70%; and if, on a 30-problem ablation, adding concept mapping, compiler-feedback repair and constraint mapping each raises the compiling rate, while proof-first anchoring, though it slightly lowers compilation, wins more paired human faithfulness comparisons than it loses.

experiments: Define the pipeline and corpora. Setup: DeepSeek-V3 generates every stage: (1) constraint explication, e.g. 'D on segment BC' becomes strict betweenness Sbtw, 'triangle ABC' adds AffineIndependent, 'line AB' adds A != B, 'circle' adds r > 0, and point order on a circle becomes a cross-product sign; (2) an informal proof sketch first, to commit to one configuration; (3) retrieval of mathlib definitions with their required side conditions; (4) compile-and-repair using Lean error messages. 32 candidates per problem. OMNI-Geometry: 780 plane-geometry problems from OMNI-Math (difficulty 1-9.5, 557 from HMMT); Numina-Geometry: 183,796 NuminaMath problems labelled geometry (32.5% olympiads, 26.2% Chinese K-12, 17.8% synthetic), a subset the official NuminaMath-Lean release excluded as too hard to formalise.

Measure coverage and expert-judged faithfulness. Result: 768 of 780 (98.5%) and 177,597 of 183,796 (96.6%) problems have at least one compiling statement. Graduate annotators with Lean experience judge 180 random OMNI-Geometry problems of difficulty >= 4 (five compiling candidates each): TOP1 / TOP5 faithful 50.94 / 77.36% (difficulty 4-5, n = 53), 55.84 / 76.62% (5-6, n = 77), 43.75 / 75.00% (6-7, n = 16), 42.11 / 57.89% (7-8, n = 19), 20.00 / 60.00% (8+, n = 15); overall 48.89 / 73.33%.

Ablate the pipeline. Setup: 30 OMNI-Geometry problems, 32 samples each (960 candidates per configuration). Result: compiling candidates 125 (13.0%) with basic prompting, 254 (26.5%) adding concept mapping, 465 (48.4%) adding compiler-feedback repair, 500 (52.1%) adding constraint mapping, 480 (50.0%) adding proof-first anchoring. A paired human Pass@3 comparison of the last two: anchoring wins 7, loses 3, 10 both correct, 10 both wrong, which the authors read as better faithfulness because anchoring adds configuration constraints whose absence would not break compilation.

Note what compilation and coverage do not show. Setup: retention counts any compiling statement, and compilation is a weak proxy for meaning; on 100 random Numina-Geometry problems, the frontier prover Aristotle refutes some statements as false, finds others trivial through misformalization or with concrete counterexamples, proves 25 and leaves 19 unresolved but unrefuted (the number filtered is not stated). Corpus-scale semantic checking is not done; the authors call Numina-Geometry a candidate corpus and note that over-strong injected hypotheses can make statements easier or vacuous. Text only: problems whose information lives in diagrams are out of scope.
